title: Letter Rack

image.credit: collection not stated on source page; via arthistoryproject.com

altText: Papers, letters and small objects appear tucked behind crossing ribbons or straps on a flat board, as if they were real items pinned to a wall. The objects are painted in muted browns, creams and soft colors with careful shadows.

source.museum: collection not stated on source page
source.verifiedBy: arthistoryproject.com artwork page text (title, medium, public-domain statement; year taken from the image file name because the page text is cut off)

context: An oil painting on canvas by Edwaert Collier. The page tags it as trompe-l'oeil, a French term for pictures designed to fool the eye into thinking the objects are real, and the page text names no collection.

descriptions.k: Letters and papers are tucked behind straps on a board. They look so real that you might want to pull one out! Which paper would you pick? What could the letter say?
descriptions.g12: Edwaert Collier painted a board with letters and papers tucked behind straps. They look so real that your eye might be tricked. Look at the edges, the shadows and the folds. Which paper looks most real to you? What clues make it seem real?
descriptions.g35: Edwaert Collier painted this Letter Rack with oil on canvas. It is a trompe-l'oeil painting, a French phrase that means trick of the eye. The letters and papers are painted so carefully that they seem to stick out from the board. Which details, such as shadows and folds, make you believe the objects are real?
descriptions.g68: Collier's Letter Rack is a trompe-l'oeil, a painting made to fool the eye into taking painted objects for real ones. Cast shadows, curling paper edges and the straps all make the flat canvas seem to have depth. This kind of picture shows off the painter's skill. How do these illusions work, and what is the pleasure of being tricked? Use the details as evidence.
descriptions.g910: Letter Rack by Collier belongs to the trompe-l'oeil tradition, in which a flat surface imitates a real object so convincingly that viewers do a double take. Shadows, curling edges and the overlap of straps and papers produce the illusion. Such works invite a game between viewer and painter. How do the formal strategies create illusion, and what does the genre suggest about painting itself? Look closely at the shadows, the edges and the straps.
descriptions.g1112: Collier's Letter Rack plays on the viewer's trust in appearances, as trompe-l'oeil does: painted paper and straps seem to occupy real space. The genre displays the artist's virtuosity and raises questions about representation and reality that painters have long explored. How does the painting use a seemingly ordinary subject to comment on illusion, and what happens to your response once you know it is flat? Weigh the evidence in the shadows, the edges and the flat surface.

k.daily: Look at the papers behind the straps. Which one looks most like a real letter?
k.emotion: How does it feel to look at something that tries to trick your eyes?

k.analysis: Which papers are tucked behind the straps, and which sit in front?
k.line: Trace the straps with your finger. Do they go straight or cross over each other?
k.shape: Papers are flat and straps are long. What other shapes can you find on the board?
k.color: The colors are soft browns and creams. Which one is your favorite in this picture?
k.texture: Imagine touching the paper and the straps. How would they feel different?
k.space: Which things look like they stick out toward you?
k.light: Look at the shadows under the papers. What do they make you think of?
k.meaning: Why might a painter want to make people think a painting is real?
k.culture: Long ago, people kept letters tucked in boards like this. How do we keep notes and messages today?
k.technique: The painter used tiny brushstrokes to make shadows. Where do you think the best shadows are?
k.personal: What secret message would you hide behind one of these straps?

g910.daily: How does the painting create a deliberate game between viewer and painter, and which devices drive it?

g1112.daily: How does Letter Rack stage the viewer's perception as part of its meaning, and when does the illusion break?
g1112.emotion: In what ways might the pleasure of being briefly fooled relate to ideas about the power and limits of painting?
g1112.observation: Scan the transitions between painted paper and the flat ground. What do they show about the painter's control of illusion?
g1112.analysis: How does the compositional logic of a flat board with attached objects differ from an open view into space?
g1112.line: How does the contrast between taut straps and soft paper edges produce tension within a restricted field?
g1112.shape: How does the reduction of the scene to a flat plane relate to later modernist interest in the picture surface?
g1112.color: How does the muted palette serve realism, and what does it withhold in comparison with more showy still life?
g1112.texture: How does the technical virtuosity of surface render the work both an object and a statement about craft?
g1112.space: How does shallow space maintain the claim that the objects are in our own world?
g1112.light: How does cast light serve both realism and the staging of a visual trick?
g1112.meaning: How might the choice of letters as a subject invite reflection on communication, privacy or absence?
g1112.culture: How did the market for painted illusions in the Dutch Republic shape what artists chose to depict?
g1112.technique: How does the lack of information about the collection and exact date affect what claims you feel able to make about the work?
g1112.personal: How does your own experience of digital images shape how you respond to a painted illusion?
g1112.critical: What would a persuasive argument look like that trompe-l'oeil is a form of play instead of a serious artistic statement, and what in the image would support or limit it?

safety.method: Image viewed and approved by the site owner (visual review) on 2026-10-18. The page text is cut off after 'in c.' so the year is not stated in the text; the date 'c. 1698' is taken from the year in the image file name supplied with the page data and should be verified by a person. The page text names no collection. The alt text and questions describe the typical trompe-l.oeil letter-rack format (papers held behind straps) and must be checked against the image. Only page text and the file name were read; the image file was not visually inspected, and a person must view the image before release.

teacherNote.context: An oil painting on canvas by Edwaert Collier, tagged as trompe-l'oeil, a style that fools the eye into seeing painted objects as real. The date c. 1698 comes from the image file name and should be checked.
directions: Have students draw an ordinary object with a strong cast shadow so it looks like it lifts off the page, then compare tricks used.
Ask students to describe how they would convince a friend a flat picture is real and test the ideas on the painting.
Discuss when it is fun to be fooled by art and when it is not.
